extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public opinion, political communication, and social psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria about how individual psychology, social conditions, and rhetorical technique combine to form public opinion and collective decisions. Useful for analyzing political rhetoric, campaigns, and theories of mass belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior as equation between variables
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern psychologists are disposed to regard the outward behavior of an adult as an equation between a number of variables, such as the resistance of the environment, repressed cravings of several maturities, and the manifest personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Kempf's formulation (manifest wishes over later repressed wishes opposed by the resistance of the environment = behavior over preadolescent repressed wishes) to emphasize that behavior is multi-causal; analysts should account for environmental resistance, multiple layers of repression, and observable personality when explaining actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repression relative to various selves
rubrics_metrics.description: The repression or control of cravings is fixed not in relation to the whole person all the time, but more or less in respect to his various selves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that different social selves (patriot, parent, employer, etc.) allow or inhibit different impulses; social situations and identities can surface buried impulses (as in psychoanalysis or crowd behavior). Explanatory models must consider situational self-construals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selves prescribe appropriate impulses (character as situational)
rubrics_metrics.description: The selves, which we construct with the help of all who influence us, prescribe which impulses, how emphasized, how directed, are appropriate to certain typical situations...For a recognizable type of experience, there is a character which controls the outward manifestations of our whole being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicting behavior or shaping moral instruction, attend to the 'prepared attitudes' associated with typical situations; examples include suppression of murderous hate in civil life and its activation in wartime—character is situationally constituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral education must prepare characters for situations
rubrics_metrics.description: The preparation of characters for all the situations in which men may find themselves is one function of a moral education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moralists must either (a) supply patterns of conduct for every life phase, or (b) prevent exposure to disapproved situations. Success depends on sincere, knowledgeable exploration of the environment; otherwise moral instruction will misfit real-world complexities (examples: teaching about war, economics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-interest is conceived and acquired (cognitive function)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary doctrine of self-interest usually omits altogether the cognitive function...men's ideas of all things and of themselves are not instinctive. They are acquired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat self-interest as an innate, fixed motive; analyses must include how individuals conceive their interests cognitively and culturally, since conceptions of interest shape behavior and can be taught or altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic situation implies probable, not specific, opinion differences
rubrics_metrics.description: From the existence of differing economic situations you can tentatively infer a probable difference of opinions, but you cannot infer what those opinions will necessarily be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use economic position as a probabilistic predictor of variance in opinion, not as a deterministic source of particular views; empirical investigation is needed to identify the content of opinions associated with economic positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of economic determinism — need special inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: In trying to explain a certain public opinion, it is rarely obvious which of a man's many social relations is effecting a particular opinion...Without special inquiry you cannot tell. The economic determinist cannot tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing opinions to economic factors, disaggregate an individual's multiple economic relations (landlord, employee, buyer, creditor, etc.) and conduct targeted inquiry; avoid simplistic one-variable explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic position predicts interests but not their form
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's various economic contacts limit or enlarge the range of his opinions. But which of the contacts, in what guise...the materialistic conception of politics cannot predict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that ownership or economic role will influence relevant opinions (e.g., owners resist deprivation) but do not infer whether that influence produces long- or short-term thinking, competitive or cooperative stances; causal form is indeterminate without further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class interest is not a single fixed conception
rubrics_metrics.description: It assumes the existence of a specific class interest. That assumption is false. A class interest can be conceived largely or narrowly, selfishly or unselfishly, in the light of no facts, some facts, many facts, truth and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject models that treat class as automatically supplying a coherent political consciousness; organizing or agitating (e.g., socialist practice) must account for variation in how class interests are conceptualized and adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal ownership will not eliminate need for education or morality
rubrics_metrics.description: A socialist state will not be able to dispense with education, morality, or liberal science, though on strict materialistic grounds the communal ownership of properties ought to make them superfluous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies assuming material conditions alone suffice to shape opinions or social order are inadequate; planners should incorporate educational and moral institutions because shared ownership does not automatically produce shared conceptions or harmonious behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instincts are shaped by experience (cognitive & affective aspects matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every instinctive act in an animal with memory must cease to be 'blind' after being once repeated...Most definitions of instincts and instinctive actions take account only of their conative aspects...it is a common mistake to ignore the cognitive and affective aspects of the instinctive mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In explaining behavior, include cognitive and affective mediation of instincts: what is feared or desired and the means used are learned; simple 'instinct' labels are insufficient for social explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human nature variability due to attachability of tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: All the important tendencies of the creature...are freely attachable to all sorts of objects as stimulus, and to all kinds of objects as gratification...each new generation is the casual victim of the way a previous generation was conditioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate great diversity in human motivations across cultures and generations; policy and persuasion must allow for different stimulus–response pairings shaped by historical conditioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion explained by techniques, not an 'oversoul'
rubrics_metrics.description: Others have concluded that since out of drift and incoherence, settled aims do appear, there must be a mysterious contrivance...But the facts can, I think, be explained more convincingly without the help of the oversoul...the art of inducing all sorts of people who think differently to vote alike is practiced in every political campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for organized techniques (rhetoric, campaigning, symbols) as the mechanisms producing unified public opinion rather than invoking mystical collective minds; analyze concrete methods leaders use to create agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for creating homogeneous votes (rhetorical tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical methods include: using 'binders' (stereotypes like 'Lincoln') to transfer piety and unity; selecting opening subjects that avoid explosive conflicts; stretching words so they 'mean all things to all men' (e.g., 'correct principles', 'American rights'); recounting neutral factual records in detail to avoid arousing opposing passions; obliterating irreconcilable issues or remaining silent on divisive future specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing political speeches or campaigns, look for these tangible tactics. Examples: Hughes invoking Lincoln to bind party factions; choosing spoils and diplomatic appointments to placate multiple groups; using ambiguous formulas to cover opposing interpretations; deliberately omitting or glossing over issues that cannot be reconciled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate decisions reflect least common denominator, not individual motives
rubrics_metrics.description: The least common denominator of all the votes was that the Democrats should go and the Republicans come in. The precise reasons why change was desired on that November day in 1920 are not recorded, not even in the memories of the individual voters...The public opinions Mr. Harding has to deal with are not the opinions that elected him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret electoral outcomes and public policy demands as products of aggregated, canceling motives; avoid assuming that election results reveal coherent, persistent collective intentions—policy-makers face a different public than the one that elected them.
